overview: This map shows one nineteenth-century interval in San Marino’s much longer history as a small republic on Mount Titano. Its 1815 and 1878 endpoints do not mark a founding or collapse. Public institutions and households occupied the same compact hilltop setting, while new associations and postal services connected residents with a changing world.

periods.title: A surviving republic
periods.summary: San Marino retained its separate institutions among the larger Italian states.

periods.title: Refuge, association and communication
periods.summary: The republic sheltered Garibaldi’s followers and later developed mutual aid and its own postage stamps.

items.text: In 1876, the Società Unione added mutual assistance for artisans and workers to its activities. Members faced the danger that illness or interrupted work could remove their income. Regular contributions created a shared fund to help when an individual household met trouble.

The society’s manifesto, dated 30 June 1876, appealed to workers’ dignity and solidarity. It argued that assistance could come from their own savings together, instead of dependence on someone else’s generosity. This document gives an unusually direct glimpse of organised social support.

The association continued after this map interval. In 1890 it established a grain store intended to supply families at controlled prices, with instalment payments and favourable interest. Access to everyday food became another practical purpose of collective help.

A postal agreement in 1865 allowed Italian stamps to be used in San Marino. The republic added its own name to the dated cancellation mark and used blue ink. Official postal history notes that Italian rules disallowed that ink because it corroded cancellation handstamps.

The date stamp bore the Italian words “REPUBBLICA DI SAN MARINO”, meaning “Republic of San Marino”. The philatelic administration transcribes this wording in its account of the 1865 arrangements. A small mark on an envelope carried the state’s identity into ordinary correspondence.

On 1 August 1877, San Marino issued its own postage stamps, printed in Turin in five values from two to forty centesimi. The 1877 agreement with Italy required each side to use its own stamps. Selling stamps also provided income for the republic.

sections.title: Building a public identity in stone

items.text: The white Carrara-marble Statue of Liberty was donated in 1876 by Countess Otilia Heyroth Wagener. Sculptor Stefano Galletti represented liberty as a woman wearing a crown of three towers. The miniature towers refer to the fortified city around the square.

The present Public Palace came later, between 1884 and 1894. Local stoneworkers were employed on its construction, while selected artisans supplied ironwork, furnishings and decoration. Its medieval-looking architecture is therefore also a record of nineteenth-century design and skilled employment.

UNESCO notes that the historic centre was extensively restored and reconstructed from the late nineteenth century into the twentieth. Some of its apparent medieval unity reflects those later choices. Meanwhile, the centre remained inhabited and continued to house the republic’s public institutions.

sections.title: A small state among large events

items.text: The two Captains Regent share the highest office of state, changing every six months. Their paired office has medieval roots. This recurring transfer of responsibilities was already a long-established institution during the nineteenth-century period shown on the map.

In 1849 Giuseppe Garibaldi arrived with about two thousand followers seeking refuge from Austrian and Roman forces. San Marino’s authorities negotiated time for them to leave. The episode placed a very small republic in the middle of Italy’s struggle over its political future.

Abraham Lincoln wrote warmly to San Marino’s Captains Regent in 1861, acknowledging the historical standing of their small state. The exchange illustrates how the republic cultivated recognition and friendship far beyond its immediate Italian neighbours.

ending.text: San Marino continued as a republic after 1878. The map’s endpoint is a coverage limit; later buildings and mutual-aid projects belong to the continuing community.
